name: How do you estimate rental return before building a multi-family project?

mainEntity.name: How can you estimate whether a new multi-family building in Los Angeles will actually produce enough rent to justify the construction cost?
mainEntity.text: How can you estimate whether a new multi-family building in Los Angeles will actually produce enough rent to justify the construction cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A strong return estimate starts with a realistic pro forma, not just the expected rent per unit. Owners should compare stabilized gross income against operating expenses, vacancy, debt service, and total development cost. In Los Angeles, the analysis should also reflect finish level, unit mix, parking, amenity package, and the local rent market for the specific neighborhood. If the building is being developed for sale rather than long-term hold, the exit value should be tested against comparable properties and capitalization assumptions. It is also important to include soft costs, carry costs, and a reserve for delays because these can materially affect the return. If the project does not support the build cost under conservative assumptions, the design may need to change before construction begins.
acceptedAnswer.description: Estimate return by comparing stabilized rent, operating costs, financing, and total project cost against expected value at completion. The key is whether the completed building will support enough income to justify land, construction, soft costs, and risk. A realistic pro forma should include vacancy, maintenance, taxes, insurance, and lease-up time.
